## Report: Does Abortion Increase Breast Cancer Risk?

**Conclusion:** The weight of scientific evidence does **not** support the claim that abortion increases breast cancer risk. The scientific consensus, as reflected by major cancer organizations, is that there is no causal link.

### Evidence Against the Claim (Stronger)

The largest and most rigorous study is the **Beral et al. (2004) collaborative reanalysis** published in *The Lancet*, which pooled individual-level data from 53 studies across 16 countries, including 83,000 women with breast cancer. It found **no association** between induced abortion and breast cancer risk ([The Lancet](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(04)15835-2/fulltext)).

The **American Cancer Society**, **Susan G. Komen**, and **Breastcancer.org** all state that the most up-to-date research shows abortion does not influence breast cancer risk ([American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html); [Susan G. Komen](https://www.komen.org/breast-cancer/facts-statistics/research-studies/topics/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk/); [Breastcancer.org](https://www.breastcancer.org/risk/risk-factors/abortion)).

A key methodological issue is **recall bias**: case-control studies relying on interviews found positive associations because women with breast cancer were more likely to report prior abortions than healthy controls. Prospective and record-based studies—which avoid this bias—consistently find no link ([JNCI, 1996](https://academic.oup.com/jnci/article/88/23/1759/914985)).

### Evidence Supporting the Claim (Weaker)

Some older **case-control studies** and certain meta-analyses—particularly those dominated by case-control designs—have reported positive associations. A 1996 meta-analysis by Brind et al. found a significant positive association across 23 studies ([JECH/BMJ](https://jech.bmj.com/content/50/5/481)). A 2014 meta-analysis of 36 Chinese studies reported a 44% increase in risk. However, these analyses are heavily influenced by studies susceptible to recall bias and confounding.

### Summary

The biological hypothesis—that interrupted pregnancy leaves breast cells in a vulnerable proliferative state—is plausible in theory, but the best epidemiological evidence, especially large prospective and record-linkage studies, does not support a real-world increased risk. The apparent associations in some studies are largely attributable to methodological biases rather than a true causal effect.
